In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Fajr (The Dawn).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the dawn﴾ ﴿and by ten nights﴾ ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾ ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾.

There has been disagreement over what is meant by "the dawn." It has been said: it is the breaking of day out of the darkness of night.

It has also been said: it is the Dawn Prayer (ṣalāt al-fajr).

Each of these two views has a witness in the Qur'an. As for the breaking of day, it is as in His saying: ﴿And by the morning when it breathes⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ ﴾ [al-Takwir: 18]. As for the Dawn Prayer, it is as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. However, the context brings the first view closer, since it concerns days and nights: "the dawn and ten nights" and "the night when it passes," all of which are time-indicating signs, to which the breaking of day is the more fitting.

After this, they differed over which dawn is intended here. It has been said that it refers generally to every dawn, and it has been said that it refers specifically to a particular dawn. The first is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them.

On the second view, it has been said: the specific dawn is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). It has also been said: the dawn of the first day of Muharram, but there is no text to rely upon. Nevertheless, the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice is closer to the ten nights, if we say that they are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, as will come, Allah willing.

As for the ten nights, the views of the exegetes are confined to: the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, the ten of Muharram, and the last ten nights of Ramadan. The first was narrated from Masruq, that they are the ten which Allah mentioned in the story of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And We completed it with ten﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. All three views are narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. There is no text in the Qur'an specifying any of them.

In the Sunnah there is an explanation of the virtue of the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the ten of Ramadan, as is well known. Since making the dawn specific to the Day of Sacrifice, the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah are closer to the context. And Allah knows best.

(p-522) ﴿And by the even and the odd﴾: The exegetes mentioned more than twenty views, and taken together they encompass all created things, in general and in detail.

As for the general view, they said: the odd (al-witr) is Allah alone, based on the hadith: "Indeed Allah is odd (witr) and loves the odd," and everything else is even (shafʿ), as in His saying: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49]. This encompasses all existence, the Creator and the created, as in the generality of ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38-39].

As for the detailed view, they said: created things are either even, like animals in pairs, the heaven, the earth, the mountain, the sea, fire, and water. Thus they mentioned for every thing its counterpart. Among things, the odd is such as air. All of these are by way of examples.

The reality, in my view, and Allah knows best, is that the closest of the views is the first, because it has been established scientifically that there is no existing being that is odd in the sense of witr at all, not even a small pebble.

For it has been established that every existing thing, whether inanimate or otherwise, is composed of atoms, and the atom has a nucleus and an orbit, and between them there is a connection, and through them occurs the explosion discovered in this age. Even in the most subtle world of industry, such as electricity: it consists of negative and positive. Likewise, there must be an electric circuit to obtain the result from any device whatsoever. Even water, which was thought to be simple, is a pair and an even, composed of two elements: oxygen and hydrogen, which separate when the temperature of water reaches one hundred, that is, boiling, and combine when the temperature falls to a certain limit, so they condense into water. And so on.

Air itself consists of several gases and compositions. Thus nothing in the universe is ever singular and odd in itself, except what the hadith states: "Indeed Allah is odd and loves the odd." The hadith may be understood to mean that the odd is He who is self-sufficient in His essence, independent of other, and one in His essence, names, attributes and acts. Thus all His attributes are odd, such as knowledge without ignorance and life without death, etc. This is unlike the created, and we said "the self-sufficient in His essence, independent of other," because every created thing is even, since each of its elements is in need of the second element so that the thing may exist with it, whereas Allah, glorified is He, is not like that. For this reason, the first view, that the odd is Allah and the even is all created things together, is the preponderant view, and it is the more general in meaning.

(p-523) The words of Allah, ﴿By the night when it passes on﴾. The exegetes agree on the meaning, which is the passing of the night, but they differ on its specification: is the intended meaning the night in general, every night, or a particular night? And which one is it?

It was said: it is general, as in His words, ﴿By the night when it withdraws﴾ [al-Takwir: 17].

It was said: it is specific, referring to the night of Muzdalifah or the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr, the night of the revelation of the Qur'an).

It is also said: if the dawn is the dawn of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), and the ten nights are the first ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah, then ﴿by the night when it passes on﴾ refers to the night of gathering (Muzdalifah). And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Al-Qurtubi and others preferred the generality of the night. In this oath He gathered all existing things, in whole and in detail, so it includes the Creator and the created, the even and the odd, both in summary and in detail: in the breaking of dawn, the dispersal of creation, the passing of the night, the stillness of the universe, and the acts of worship during the ten nights.

Among the greatest oaths Allah swore by is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr: 5]. That is, for one of intellect. The root ḥ-j-r (ḥ-j-r) revolves around firmness and strength. Thus al-ḥajar (ḥajar, "stone") is named for its strength; al-ḥujrah (ḥujrah, "chamber") for the firmness of what is within it. Intellect is called ḥijr (ḥijr, with a kasra on the ḥ) because it restrains its possessor from what is unbecoming. Al-maḥjūr ʿalayh (the one placed under restriction) is so called because he is prevented from disposing of his affairs and from securing them. A woman's ḥajr over her child (her guardianship) is similar. So, are these five things sworn by a sufficient oath for one of intellect? The answer is yes, and this without doubt strengthens this oath.

Then the scholars differed concerning the answer to this oath, since He, exalted is He, did not state it explicitly as He did in its parallel, His saying: ﴿So I swear by the setting-places of the stars, and indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 75–76]. He then stated the sworn matter: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 77]. Here He did not state it despite the greatness of the oath, so the disagreement arose over its specification.

It was said: it is implied, its estimated form being "Surely He will punish," indicated by His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 6–13].

It was said: it is present, and it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. Al-Qurtubi said this.

From the standpoint of grammatical craft (ṣināʿah, the technical discipline of Arabic grammar) in the language and the methods of exegesis, this is sound. But in my view, and Allah the Exalted knows best, there is a connection between the oath and its answer, and between what comes at the end of the surah, His saying: ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded﴾ [al-Fajr: 21] to the end of the surah.

Likewise, a great connection appears between it and the end of the surah before it, for in that surah came: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller, except one who turns away and disbelieves. Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 21–24]. And: ﴿By the dawn. And by ten nights. And the even and the odd. And the night when it passes﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr: 1–5]. This is because what it contains of the warning of the greatest punishment, and of their return to Allah alone and His reckoning of them alone, is fittingly matched by this great oath.

As for its connection with what is at the end of the surah: the things sworn by here are five named things: ﴿By the dawn﴾, ﴿and ten nights﴾, ﴿and the even and the odd﴾, ﴿and the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 1–4]. And what is at the end of the surah is also five named things: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded﴾, ﴿and your Lord comes with the angels, rank upon rank﴾, ﴿and Hell is brought that Day; on that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ [al-Fajr: 21–23].

These are scenes that encompass the entire Last Day, from the first blowing of the Trumpet, through the pounding of the earth, to the end of the reckoning and every person's remembrance of what he owes and what is owed against him. They correspond to what the preceding oath included of the affairs of this world.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 89, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd,﴾ ﴿Iram of the pillars,﴾ ﴿the like of whom had not been created in the lands,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, who hewed the rocks in the valley,﴾ ﴿and Pharaoh, the lord of stakes,﴾ ﴿who committed excess in the lands?﴾

Here it does not specify what He did, nor how, to those they mention, namely ʿĀd, Thamud, and Pharaoh.

The mention of all three has already occurred in surah "al-Haqqah," at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast,﴾ ﴿and as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind,﴾ ﴿which He unleashed against them,﴾ up to His saying ﴿so He seized them with a terrible seizing﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5–10].

What is new here is the description of each: that ʿĀd are "of the pillars," that "the like of them was not created in the lands," that Thamud "hewed the rocks in the valley," and that Pharaoh is "the lord of stakes."

Regarding the meaning of these descriptions, differing views have been stated:

As for ʿĀd, it was said: the "pillars" are the poles of tents of hair (goat-hair tents), and what is meant is the tribe. The height of the poles of their tents is a metaphor for the height of their bodies, as was said of Ṣakhr in the line:

*Lofty of pillar, long of sword-belt.*

And the height of bodies indicates the strength of their owners.

It was also said: Iram was a city of lofty buildings. They related about its reports stories that exceed imagination, and that it is in the Empty Quarter. But since its reports were not established by a chain of transmission on which one can rely, and reality did not confirm it, some people said: it has been swallowed up by the earth and no longer exists.

As for Thamud: they "hewed," that is, carved the rock in the valley, the Valley of the Villages (Wadi al-Qura) among the cities of Ṣāliḥ, and their houses still exist to this day.

As for Pharaoh, "the lord of stakes": it was said: they are tent-stakes, which he would drive for those he tortured.

It was also said: it is a metaphor for the armies by which he secured his kingdom.

It was also said: they are high mounds and lofty walls, where games were played for him in their open spaces.

Ibn Jarir said, and his text is: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and Pharaoh, the lord of stakes﴾: it was mentioned to us that they were platforms and playgrounds, under which games were played for him, made of stakes and mountains.

What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that this view is the correct one, that they are lofty structures, and that they are the ones now known as the Pyramids in Egypt. Several matters support this:

Among them: they resemble stakes in their appearance, with one end pointing upward, since the summit is like the head of a stake, sharply pointed relative to their massiveness. Thus they are triangular in shape, with the base downward and the apex upward.

Among them: their mention alongside Thamud, who hewed the rock in the valley, given the common features of might. Those carved the rock into splendid houses, while these cut huge rock from a place with no mountains around it, which indicates that it was transported from a distant place. The reality is that they are large blocks, great boulders, so in quarrying them, in transporting them to the site of their construction, and in the construction itself, all of this indicates strength and tyranny, and the subjugation of people for that purpose.

Among them: interpreting them as the Pyramids, which stand in their own right and are observed in every age and by every generation, is more effective in admonition and reflection: that He who destroyed those nations is able to destroy the deniers among the Quraysh and others.

The Mighty Lord has spoken truly: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 89, verse 15:

Allah's saying: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and bestows favours upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him and restricts his provision for him, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ ﴿No!﴾

He (may He be exalted) explains that He gives and withholds as a trial (ibtila') for the servant.

As for His saying, "No!" (kalla), it is a word of reproach and repulsion, and a clarification that the meaning is not as you have said. It corrects the notions of the disbelievers: that giving and withholding are neither a sign of honour nor a sign of humiliation, but a trial (ibtila'), as in His saying: ﴿Every soul shall taste death, and We test you with evil and good as a trial.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]

And His saying: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitnah).﴾ [al-Anfal: 28]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 89, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾ ﴿nor urge one another to feed the poor﴾ ﴿and you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with an intense love﴾. After He, glorified is He, had explained the correct understanding of giving and withholding, these verses came and explained the reality of the trial of wealth, both in acquiring and in spending, in gathering and in dispensing. He began with the most ugly aspects of withholding: failing to honour the orphan, who has a broken wing and a wounded heart, and holding back from feeding the poor, who is empty-handed, hungry in the belly, and still in motion. These two aspects are the most important tasks of spending wealth, and they withhold from them. Allah, exalted is He, explained that this aspect is "breaking through the steep path" in times of hardship, in His saying in Surah "al-Balad": ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you know what the steep path is? It is freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of severe hunger an orphan near of relationship, or a poor man in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 11-16].

And from the other side: ﴿and you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily﴾, i.e., the inheritance. So they do not give the women, who are weak in personality and more in need of the wealth of their deceased relative. And you love wealth with an intense love, to the point that it has enslaved you and the multiplication of it has distracted you.

Here is a reminder to both groups: whoever has been given should not neglect the important avenues of spending, and whoever has been withheld from should not aspire to what is not fitting for him. And success is with Allah, exalted is He.

(p. 527) The words of the Exalted: ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded and crushed﴾ ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels in rows, row upon row﴾.

This same context has already been mentioned in Surat al-Haqqah, after the mention of Thamud, 'Ad and Pharaoh, in His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown with one blast, and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single crushing, [then on that Day the Event will come to pass]... and the angels will be upon its extremities﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13-17]. This clarifies the meaning of ﴿row upon row﴾, i.e., upon its extremities, row after row.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had previously referred, for its explanation, to Surat al-Rahman at His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]. And His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels in rows﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]. ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ is among the verses of the Attributes (ayat al-sifat).

Points of inquiry and consideration:

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has repeatedly discussed in Adwa' al-Bayan in several places the matter of these [attributes]. It should be known that this, along with istiwa' (settling/establishment), the hadith of descent (hadith al-nuzul), and the coming (al-ityan) mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud with the angels, and the matter be decided? And to Allah are all matters returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has also presented the topic of the verses of the Attributes in full in a lecture he titled "Ayat al-Sifat" (The Verses of the Attributes), which was published separately.

As he had previously stated, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in Surat al-A'raf at His saying: ﴿Then He settled upon the Throne, covering the night with the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], although he did not address the attribute of coming (al-maji') in itself, he did say that all the attributes are of one category, meaning that they are affirmed for Allah, the Exalted, upon the principle of: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11], without any likeness to created beings. Thus istiwa' befitting His majesty is affirmed without any likeness to created beings.

Likewise here: just as istiwa' is affirmed, so is coming (maji') affirmed, and just as coming is affirmed, so is descent (nuzul) affirmed.

All of this falls under the principle of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, i.e., as al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "We are charged with belief (iman), so it is incumbent upon us to believe in the attributes of Allah in the manner befitting Allah and in accordance with Allah's intent. It is not incumbent upon us to ask how (takyif), for the how (kayf) is prohibited concerning Allah, glorified be He."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Fajr

The Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angel, rank upon rank﴾.

This gives the impression that it is one angel, while His saying ﴿rank upon rank﴾ requires that it is not a single angel but ranks of groups of angels.

The answer is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the angel﴾ means "and the angels." Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the angels will be upon its sides﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17]. Its explanation, with its Arabic evidences, has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29] and what follows it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 89, verse 23:

(p-528) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾

He, may He be exalted, has already explained the subject of man's remembrance, which is His saying: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life."﴾ [al-Fajr: 24].

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us) has already given the explanation of this in Surat al-Furqan, at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken with the Messenger a way."﴾ [al-Furqan: 27] and the verses that follow.
